---
title: Amending a Run
llms-description: "A Steward workspace is a project rather than a single run: how editing the definition and launching again converges toward new desired state, which edits create work and which do not, and why removing work needs your explicit acceptance."
---

## Overview

The word *run* invites a model Steward does not have — a thing that starts, has
an identity, and ends. What a workspace actually holds is a **project**: one
definition that evolves, one log directory accumulating its results, one archive
holding everything superseded, and one journal recording what was decided.

Work happens in episodes, but an episode is not an entity. Nothing keys on one,
nothing is named after one, and none needs an id. So there is no *amend*
command, and no *resume* command either. There is only:

> Edit the definition, and run `steward launch` again.

## Why that works

Steward is a control loop, and the pieces line up exactly:

``` text
manifest (from the definition)  =  desired state
log directory                   =  observed state
steward tend                    =  the controller
```

`launch` captures a new desired state; every turn after it drives the log
directory toward that state. Anything already satisfying it is left alone.
Nothing is re-derived and nothing is re-paid for.

This is not a mechanism Steward invents. It is what `eval_set()` has always done
when pointed at the same log directory twice, and Steward inherits it by
inheriting the boundary.

## Which edits create work

You do not have to reason about this, and that is the point — Inspect already
answers two separate questions, and the separation does all the work:

-   **Is this the same task?** Answered by a task's identity, which covers its
    file, name, arguments, model, resolved solver, generate config, and
    execution limits.
-   **Has enough of it been done?** Answered by comparing sample counts against
    epochs and the dataset limit, both of which are held deliberately *outside*
    that identity.

So an edit sorts itself into one of four outcomes with no policy from Steward at
all:

| you change | identity | what happens |
|----|----|----|
| add a task, add a model | new tasks appear | new work; existing logs untouched |
| a task argument, the solver, generate config, a task limit | **changes** | a *different* task — new work, and the previous log is superseded |
| `epochs`, the dataset `limit` | **stable** | the *same* task, now incomplete — it resumes and adds only the missing samples |
| nothing | stable | everything no-ops |

The third row is what makes extending a project cheap rather than merely
possible. Raising epochs from 1 to 3 reuses the epoch-1 samples and runs epochs
2 and 3, because resume matches samples on id *and* epoch.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Extending by epochs needs no new mechanism, and cannot have one — nothing can
add work to a running eval. A worker already in flight is left alone; its log
lands, reads as incomplete, and the next turn resumes it. What that produces is
epoch 1, which is precisely what the extension reuses, so letting it finish is
right rather than merely tolerable. The cost is latency: a task six hours from
finishing starts its new epochs in six hours.
:::

## One trigger, and one gate on it

Capture executes your definition, so it is expensive — and more importantly, the
definition is a file you edit live. Anything that captured automatically would
eventually capture a half-saved edit. So the division is sharp:

| verb | reads the definition? | |
|----|----|----|
| `steward launch` | **yes** | captures a fresh manifest, reports the delta, commits it, spawns |

Re-launching reuses the arguments you last launched with, so forgetting a `-A`
cannot quietly capture a different eval set. `--no-args` is how you go back to
the definition's own defaults.
| `steward tend` | no | converges toward the *stored* manifest |
| `steward status` | no | reports state, and whether the definition has drifted since capture |

Drift detection is free — one hash of the file against the one the manifest
recorded — so an edit is **never silently ignored**. It shows up in the
attention list as `drift`, with `steward launch` as the command that resolves
it.

### Removing work needs you to say so

Adding work is what you just asked for. Removing it could equally be a typo — a
one-character change to a task argument is indistinguishable from a deliberate
removal, and it quietly buys a re-run of everything downstream. So `launch`
reports its delta and treats the two asymmetrically:

``` text
launching would:
  add        3 tasks                                (1,500 samples)
  extend    40 tasks   epochs 1 → 3                 (12,000 samples)
  restore    2 tasks   already run by this project  (1,000 samples, 2 logs)
  archive   12 tasks   removed from the definition  (6,000 samples, 12 logs, 2 workers stopped)
  archive    8 tasks   args changed → superseded    (4,000 samples, 8 logs)

Error: 20 tasks would leave logs/. Nothing has been committed — pass
--accept-archive to proceed.
```

A purely additive delta proceeds — `add`, `extend`, and `restore` all commit
without being asked. Anything that would cost you results requires explicit
acceptance, and until you give it **nothing about the run has been written**:
not the manifest, not the logs, not the journal. The refusal exits non-zero, so
a script notices it too.

There are two ways to cost yourself results, and only the first shows up as a
row:

``` text
launching would:
  the log directory moves: logs → results
    18 tasks with results in the old one would run again in the new one, and
    those results would be left where they are
    4 workers still writing to the old one would be stopped
```

Changing `log_dir` in your definition leaves every task identity untouched, so
the table is empty and the edit looks like the safest thing you could do — while
committing it re-runs the whole sweep into the new directory and abandons what
is in the old one. Steward gates it with the same flag for the same reason.

Anything still running is stopped, because a worker's destination is fixed when
it starts: after the move it would spend hours writing a log nothing reads, and
its task would start again from nothing once it finished. If what you meant was
*move the run*, copy the logs across first — a task whose results are already in
the new directory will not run again.

Two of those rows are worth reading closely. **`extend` is not a re-run**:
raising `epochs` keeps a task's identity, so the work already in `logs/` still
counts and the next turn resumes rather than starting over. And **archiving a
task something is still running stops that worker first** — asked through its
control channel rather than killed, so the samples it has already finished land
in the log before it is archived.

The same asymmetry bounds what an agent supervising your run may do unasked: it
may commit an additive delta, because you typed the instruction and asking
whether you meant it is the interruption Steward exists to remove. Anything that
archives escalates, always ([Working with an Agent](agents.qmd)).

## Nothing is ever deleted

A log leaving `logs/` is **always a move, never a delete** — reversible, and
recorded with its reason. Superseded, removed, and failed logs go to a sibling
`logs-archive/` directory.

Three situations turn out to be the same operation:

| a log leaves `logs/` because | |
|----|----|
| its task was **removed** from the definition | archived |
| its task was **superseded** by an edit that changed its identity | archived |
| it is a **failed attempt** replaced by a good one | archived |

That third row is the one worth noticing: `eval_set()` deletes those. Folding it
in means Steward never deletes an eval log — a simple, checkable property for a
tool asked to be trusted with unattended expensive work.

What it buys is a precise meaning for the log directory that it did not have
before: **`logs/` is the current definition's results and nothing else.** That is
what makes `samples_df("logs")` trustworthy without anyone remembering a filter.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
`logs-archive/` is a *sibling* of `logs/` rather than a subdirectory, because
log discovery recurses by default — an archive underneath `logs/` would hide
nothing from `samples_df()` or the viewer.
:::

### The archive is also a cache

Edit a task's arguments, launch, decide the edit was wrong, revert — the
original identity comes back, and a matching log is sitting in the archive.
Restoring it is a move rather than a re-run, so revert-after-edit is free.

The archive grows and never shrinks, which on object storage is a real bill.
That is yours to lifecycle-rule. Steward offers no prune verb, because a command
whose job is deleting results is precisely the one this design exists to avoid.

## A mid-edit save is not a hazard

Worth stating because it sounds like one. If you launch while a definition is
half-edited, one of three things happens, and none is harmful:

-   **Syntactically broken** — capture fails, and nothing is committed.
-   **Valid but additive** — it gets applied early, and the next launch picks up
    the rest. The final state is right; only the start is staggered, because
    convergence is forgiving that way.
-   **Valid but wrong** — harmful only if it archives, and that is gated.
